lesson.title: Cooperation Before the Ballot: How the Farmers' Alliance Built a Movement
lesson.summary: Years before Populist candidates ever appeared on a ballot, hundreds of thousands of farmers organized cooperative buying and selling networks through the Farmers' Alliance, the grassroots organization that became the seedbed of the Populist Party.
lesson.body:
The People's Party did not appear out of nowhere. It grew directly out of the Farmers' Alliance, a network of local farmer organizations that spread rapidly across the South and the Plains in the 1870s and 1880s. The movement began in Texas in the late 1870s, a response to falling cotton and grain prices, and to the crop lien system, which forced many farmers to borrow against next year's harvest from local merchants at punishing interest rates just to buy seed and supplies, trapping them in debt that grew faster than they could pay it off.

The Alliance was not a single organization. The Southern Farmers' Alliance operated across the former Confederacy, a separate Northwestern Alliance organized farmers on the northern Plains, and because Jim Crow segregation barred Black farmers from joining the white Southern Alliance, a distinct Colored Farmers' National Alliance and Cooperative Union organized Black tenant farmers and sharecroppers separately, even as many of their economic grievances overlapped closely with those of white Alliance members.

The Alliance's central strategy was economic cooperation. Local chapters organized cooperative stores and grain elevators so members could buy supplies in bulk and sell crops collectively, bypassing the merchants and grain buyers who otherwise controlled both ends of the transaction and captured much of the value of a farmer's labor. Alliance leader Charles Macune, based in Texas, also developed the subtreasury plan, a proposal for federal warehouses where farmers could store nonperishable crops as collateral for low interest government loans, letting them avoid selling their entire harvest immediately after it came in, when prices were always at their lowest. Congress never adopted the plan.

By the late 1880s, many of the Alliance's cooperative ventures were struggling, undercapitalized and facing resistance from the railroads and wholesalers whose profits they threatened. Alliance leaders increasingly concluded that only direct political action could address problems rooted in national monetary policy and railroad regulation, forces no local cooperative could overcome on its own. That conclusion produced the Ocala Demands of 1890 and, in 1892, the Alliance's transformation into the political backbone of the newly formed People's Party at its Omaha convention.
